New Orleans elevation and population figures are unusually volatile even by that standard — much of the city sits at or below sea level, and population has fluctuated significantly since Hurricane Katrina (2005), so these numbers should be treated as rough until replaced.

visitWindow.note: Inter-trip interlude, not a numbered leg of Trip 1 or Trip 2 — sits between Austin (Trip 1 end) and Austin (Trip 2 start). Mardi Gras Day fell on Feb 17, 2026, inside this window. Functions as the residency-analysis micro-residency control case; excluded from the core self-curation vs. sourced-curation thesis since no guide was built at the time of the stay.

framing: New Orleans sits outside the trip's central experiment entirely — it's the gap between Trip 1's self-curated leg and Trip 2's sourced-curation leg, visited during Mardi Gras with no guide produced at the time. This guide was built retroactively, six months after the stay, purely as a reference and as a companion to the residency-analysis micro-residency control case. Where it does connect to the trip's other analytical threads: Congo Square and Dooky Chase's both sit on the same civil-rights-history throughline as the Southern corridor's Black business districts, though the erasure mechanism here (a cultural origin-point overshadowed by tourism narratives, rather than a district razed by a specific highway or urban-renewal project) is different enough from the confirmed corridor pattern that it's flagged as tentative rather than folded in directly.

analyticalThread.summary: Proposed, unconfirmed instance. Congo Square (birthplace of the musical traditions that became jazz) and Dooky Chase's Restaurant (a real civil rights-era meeting place) both carry civil-rights and Black-cultural-origin weight, but the mechanism differs from every confirmed corridor carrier: there is no single highway, urban-renewal project, or riot-aftermath event that erased a business district here. The erosion, if it's the same phenomenon at all, runs through tourism-narrative flattening and municipal neglect (most visibly in the Lower 9th Ward post-Katrina) rather than a specific demolition event. Flagged for Greg's review before treating this as a confirmed carrier of the thread — similar in spirit to Shreveport's own unconfirmed proposal.

locations.name: Lafayette Cemetery No. 1
locations.note: Anne Rice's own cemetery of choice; provided much of the film's Gothic atmosphere and has appeared in numerous other productions since.

locations.name: French Quarter (various streets)
locations.note: General Gothic backdrop for the film's 18th-century New Orleans sequences.

locations.name: LaLaurie Mansion
locations.address: 1140 Royal St, French Quarter, New Orleans, LA
locations.note: Private residence — exterior view only. Named for the historical Madame LaLaurie, whose house is one of the most infamous in the French Quarter.

locations.name: Lafayette Cemetery No. 1
locations.note: Site of a jazz-funeral scene in Episode 10.

locations.name: Hermann-Grima House
locations.note: Featured location for several Coven scenes.

locations.name: Audubon Park
locations.note: One of several New Orleans locations used alongside River Road plantations (Felicity Plantation).

locations.name: The Columns Hotel
locations.address: St. Charles Ave, New Orleans, LA
locations.note: Historic Garden District hotel used as a filming location.

locations.name: Café Du Monde
locations.address: 800 Decatur St, French Quarter, New Orleans, LA
locations.note: Recurring background location across the series' run (2014–2021).

films.title: The Curious Case of Benjamin Button

locations.name: Nolan House
locations.address: 2707 Coliseum St, Garden District, New Orleans, LA
locations.note: Where the bulk of the film's nursing-home scenes were shot; the house has since sold privately.

notablePeople.name: Louis Armstrong
notablePeople.note: Jazz's foundational figure, born and raised in New Orleans; Congo Square and Louis Armstrong Park carry his legacy directly.

notablePeople.name: Anne Rice
notablePeople.note: Author of The Vampire Chronicles (Interview with the Vampire, 1976); drew directly on New Orleans cemeteries and Catholic upbringing for her Gothic fiction. Buried near Metairie/Lake Lawn Cemetery.

notablePeople.name: Truman Capote
notablePeople.note: Southern Gothic novelist (In Cold Blood, Breakfast at Tiffany's); born in New Orleans but raised largely in Alabama.

notablePeople.name: Jelly Roll Morton
notablePeople.note: Composer and pianist who claimed to have "invented jazz" in 1902; foundational early-jazz figure.

notablePeople.name: Phil Anselmo
notablePeople.note: Hardcore-adjacent heavy metal vocalist (Pantera, Down, Superjoint); direct connection to the traveler's punk/hardcore interest.

notablePeople.name: Big Freedia
notablePeople.note: Bounce-music artist and queer icon, a distinctly New Orleans musical export.

recommendations.name: Faulkner House Books
recommendations.note: William Faulkner lived here in 1925 while writing his first novel; now a small shop specializing in Southern literary classics and rare first editions.

recommendations.name: Baldwin & Co.
recommendations.address: 1030 Elysian Fields Ave, New Orleans, LA
recommendations.note: Black-owned bookstore and coffee shop built around social justice and Black authors, with a packed author-events calendar and a small in-house recording studio.

recommendations.name: Community Book Center
recommendations.note: Decades-old Black-owned institution on Bayou Road's historic Black business corridor — African-centered titles, gifts, and deep community standing.

recommendations.name: Iron Rail Book Collective
recommendations.address: 4210 St. Claude Ave, New Orleans, LA
recommendations.note: Mandatory infoshop pick: volunteer-run anarchist lending library and zine archive (3,000+ titles, plus the Above Ground Zine Library), now housed inside the CANOA arts/music venue.

recommendations.name: Rank & File Books
recommendations.note: Radical, anarchist, and feminist bookstore and zine shop sharing space with Sisters in Christ Records and Mae's Guitars.

recommendations.name: Louisiana Music Factory
recommendations.note: The city's essential local-music specialist — deep jazz, brass band, R&B, and Mardi Gras Indian catalog, with a crate-digging vinyl room upstairs.

recommendations.name: Euclid Records
recommendations.note: Two floors of new and used vinyl, CDs, and 45s, a bit off the tourist track and locally called "the best record store in town."

recommendations.name: Domino Sound Record Shack
recommendations.note: Opened 2007 on the Bayou Road Black business corridor, a serious crate-digger favorite with strong reggae and international selections.

recommendations.name: Sisters in Christ Records
recommendations.note: Metal-leaning vinyl curation, sharing its space with Rank & File Books.

recommendations.name: NOLA Mix Records
recommendations.note: A small shop with a tightly curated, well-loved selection on Magazine St.

recommendations.name: Café Du Monde
recommendations.note: Chicory café au lait and sugar-dusted beignets since 1862 — the essential New Orleans coffee stop.

recommendations.name: Congregation Coffee Roasters
recommendations.note: Local roaster working ethically sourced single-origin coffee.

recommendations.name: Baldwin & Co.
recommendations.address: 1030 Elysian Fields Ave, New Orleans, LA
recommendations.note: Cross-listed with Bookstores — coffee program plus a small in-house recording studio in a Black-owned, social-justice-minded space.

recommendations.name: HiVolt Coffee
recommendations.note: The Bywater's independent-spirit coffee anchor, a neighborhood mainstay for coffee-with-food.

recommendations.name: Mammoth Espresso
recommendations.note: Dialed-in espresso bar frequently praised by Eater and Thrillist.

recommendations.name: Croissant D'Or Patisserie
recommendations.note: Classic French-technique pastry shop, laminated dough done right.

recommendations.name: Ayu Bakehouse
recommendations.note: Its Croissant City Classic King Cake won the Times-Picayune's 2025 king cake bracket over 320,000 votes cast; also known for the cro madame.

recommendations.name: Bywater Bakery
recommendations.note: Long Carnival-season king cake lines, Breakfast Gumbo, and community-minded owners active in mutual aid.

recommendations.name: Dong Phuong Bakery
recommendations.address: 14207 Chef Menteur Hwy, New Orleans, LA
recommendations.note: Vietnamese-American bakery with a dominant king cake reputation citywide; a drive from the core.

recommendations.name: Levee Baking Co.
recommendations.note: Croissants and sweet breads with lines that back up the quality claim.

recommendations.name: Muffuletta — Central Grocery & Deli
recommendations.note: Invented here in 1906 by Sicilian grocer Salvatore Lupo; the round Italian loaf stacked with cured meats, cheese, and olive salad that judges every muffuletta after it.

recommendations.name: Gumbo — Dooky Chase's Restaurant
recommendations.note: Restaurant helmed for decades by "Queen of Creole Cuisine" Leah Chase, and a real civil rights-era meeting place beyond its food.

recommendations.name: Sazerac — Sazerac Bar, Roosevelt Hotel
recommendations.note: Rye whiskey, Peychaud's Bitters, and absinthe — America's oldest cocktail, official cocktail of New Orleans since 2008.

recommendations.name: Bananas Foster — Brennan's
recommendations.note: Tableside flambé dessert invented at Brennan's in 1951 by chef Paul Blangé, still the house signature.

recommendations.name: New Orleans-Style BBQ Shrimp — Pascal's Manale
recommendations.note: Head-on shrimp in a rich black-pepper butter sauce, invented here in the mid-1950s and, despite the name, entirely unrelated to barbecue.

recommendations.name: Crystal Hot Sauce
recommendations.note: The hot sauce locals actually reach for over Tabasco, made in New Orleans since the 1920s.

recommendations.name: Peychaud's Bitters
recommendations.note: The bitters that built the Sazerac, invented by a French Quarter apothecary — a cocktail-themed gift with a direct whiskey-history tie.

recommendations.name: Tony Chachere's / Slap Ya Mama
recommendations.note: Shelf-stable Creole and Cajun seasoning blends that are genuine kitchen staples here, not tourist product.

recommendations.name: What It Bees Like Honey
recommendations.note: Urban beekeeper Shae Thomas harvests directly from hives in the Gentilly Woods neighborhood — genuinely in-city honey, not regional.

recommendations.name: Zatarain's New-Orleans-in-a-Box
recommendations.note: Gumbo, jambalaya, and red beans & rice packaged as shelf-stable mixes since 1889.

recommendations.name: Congo Square
recommendations.note: Where enslaved and free Black New Orleanians gathered on Sundays to play music, dance, and trade — the literal birthplace of the rhythms that became jazz.
recommendations.filmConnection: NCIS: New Orleans recurring backdrop (as Louis Armstrong Park)

recommendations.name: Museum of Death
recommendations.note: Oddities collection including Dr. Kevorkian's Thanatron — the city's most concentrated horror/occult stop.

recommendations.name: Rice Family Mausoleum / Lafayette Cemetery No. 1
recommendations.note: Anne Rice's resting place and the real-world set for jazz-funeral scenes in Interview with the Vampire and American Horror Story: Coven.
recommendations.filmConnection: Interview with the Vampire (1994); American Horror Story: Coven (2013)

recommendations.name: Carousel Bar, Hotel Monteleone
recommendations.note: The only rotating bar in the city, spinning since 1949, and the birthplace of the rye-whiskey Vieux Carré cocktail.

recommendations.name: Jean Lafitte National Historical Park (Barataria Preserve)
recommendations.note: 26,000 free, boardwalked acres of bayou, swamp, and marsh 25 minutes south of downtown — alligators and free ranger-led tours included.

recommendations.name: Fred Hampton Free Store
recommendations.address: 5523 St. Claude Ave, New Orleans, LA
recommendations.note: Mutual-aid free store, skate rink, and punk show venue named for the Black Panther chairman — explicitly "the only all-ages venue in Greater New Orleans."

recommendations.name: Siberia
recommendations.address: 2227 St. Claude Ave, New Orleans, LA
recommendations.note: Bar/venue self-described by regulars as a "hardcore metal/punk refuge."

recommendations.name: Gasa Gasa
recommendations.note: Booking venue that's a longtime scene favorite among local punk and indie writers.

recommendations.name: Saturn Bar
recommendations.note: Dive-bar institution with a long-running punk and garage booking history.

recommendations.name: Midcity Ballroom
recommendations.note: Hosts touring hardcore/metal DIY bills, often presented by Louisiana Hardcore; the city's DIY show calendar and booking collective (Belly Up) live at noladiy.org alongside the Free Store.

recommendations.name: Home Malone
recommendations.note: "Where locals shop local" — stationery and magnets by New Orleans artist Kristin Malone, plus local jewelry and ceramics.

recommendations.name: Palace Market
recommendations.note: Frenchmen St alley market of independent local artists and artisans — prints, jewelry, and NOLA-pun T-shirts.

recommendations.name: Dr. Bob's Folk Art
recommendations.note: Outsider folk art from the artist behind the citywide "Be Nice Or Leave" signs — a genuinely only-in-New-Orleans souvenir.

recommendations.name: Frenchmen Art Bazaar
recommendations.note: Open-air market of local prints and crafts alongside the live-music strip.

recommendations.name: Gallery Rinard
recommendations.note: Local prints gallery, including posters from Barkus, the city's dog Mardi Gras parade.

recommendations.name: Community Workshop NOLA (The Workshop)
recommendations.note: Queer-led, female-founded cooperative makerspace with 24/7 member access and open community classes.

recommendations.name: NOLA Guitar Shop
recommendations.address: 3920 General De Gaulle Dr, New Orleans, LA
recommendations.note: Post-Katrina (2005) shop stocking guitars, amps, and Eurorack modular synthesizers — the closest thing here to a dedicated synth shop, with proceeds supporting youth music programs.

recommendations.name: FabLab NOLA (Delgado Community College)
recommendations.address: 615 City Park Ave, New Orleans, LA
recommendations.note: Laser cutters, CNC routers, a vinyl cutter, and 3D printers, open to community members and small businesses, not just students.

recommendations.name: Strange Guitarworks
recommendations.note: Full-service guitar repair and luthier shop doing everything from restringing to electronics work and full restorations.

recommendations.name: NolaWorks
recommendations.note: General wood/auto/metal makerspace with classes — honest evidence that the city's maker scene leans fabrication over electronics.

statusNotes.text: Iron Rail Book Collective operated as unhoused pop-ups for years before relocating into CANOA at 4210 St. Claude Ave in April 2026 — after the Feb 2026 visit window, so no fixed storefront existed during the actual stay.
Rank & File Books' current operating hours at its Sisters in Christ/Mae's Guitars location are unconfirmed in available sources — call or check socials ahead of a visit.

honestGaps.text: New Orleans' maker scene leans wood/metal/textile fabrication, not dedicated electronics or hackerspace culture — no Arduino/Raspberry Pi hackerspace with published open-hours turned up in research. NOLA Guitar Shop's Eurorack modular-synth stock is the closest genuine electronics-culture touchpoint the city offers.

scopeDecision: New Orleans-proper primary; Jean Lafitte National Historical Park (Barataria Preserve) and Dong Phuong Bakery included as the two out-of-core-city exceptions, both flagged in their own entries as involving travel time.
